items.title: Ron Carter — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: As my name became highlighted, I'd been in the Miles band

ctx.x: Okay. I'm not clear on the chronology, but at some point you began to do some – you were recording all the time – but I think you also got into sort of TV and commercial recording.

That came during the course of my time with Miles. At the time New York was bustling with recording. There were like twelve jazz labels or so. People from Japan would come all the time, they'd work with the musicians and then be off, and then there was just stuff to do. As my name became highlighted, I'd been in the Miles band, all the commercial writers who are into that musical zone wanted to get the rhythm section or one of us on their commercial. So it was … the only thing I had to do was go out and do the job.
I was fascinated to read about your disagreement with Harold Mayburn.

items.title: Ron Carter interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: We’d been off about four months, and he told us this is a benefit. So maybe I guess I was the spokesperson of the band said

ctx.x: That was done at Lincoln Center. People don’t realize that Miles was a real civil activist and he would often play for these civil rights fundraisers. And that night was a fundraiser for some civil rights group, I can’t remember, NAACP or something like that. We’d been off about four months, and he told us this is a benefit. So maybe I guess I was the spokesperson of the band said, it’s a benefit, okay, well why don’t you benefit them and let us have our money? And if I decide I want to benefit them I’ll give…
